title: TS SDK: graceful stream swap adapter for async iterator / Web Streams compatibility
creator: Aisha Park
description:
Problem: Consumers sometimes need to transparently switch the underlying data source mid-consumption (for example: fallback from hosted model stream to a dedicated/private model stream, or reconnect after transient transport failure) without breaking async iterator or Web Stream semantics. Current patterns either close the consumer and require re-consumption from the application layer or rely on brittle ad-hoc bridges that lose backpressure/cancellation semantics.

Proposal: Implement a lightweight TS SDK adapter (StreamSwapAdapter) that exposes a stable AsyncIterable and a Web Streams ReadableStream facade, and allows the runtime to swap the underlying source during active consumption. The adapter preserves ordering, provides configurable draining behavior for the old source (drain remainder vs drop), preserves backpressure semantics to the extent possible, and propagates cancellation and AbortSignals across sources. The adapter should be small, testable, and play well with our existing stream bridging utilities in the SDK.

Goals: safe mid-stream swap, minimal API surface, strong test coverage across Node/Deno/Browser, clear examples and docs for customers and example apps.
acceptance_criteria: Adapter exposes AsyncIterable<T> and asReadableStream(): ReadableStream<T> with consistent semantics
Support swap(newSource, options) where options include drainPolicy := [drain, drop] and checkpoint token
Cancellation via returned AbortController/Signal cancels all current and future underlying sources
No observable duplication or loss for common swap scenarios (fall back, reconnect, model variant switch) under tests
Unit + integration tests that cover Node/Deno/Browser runtimes, backpressure and cancellation
Documentation: API reference, migration notes, and two canonical examples (fallback on reconnect, model-variant swap)
technical_design:
High-level: the adapter internally maintains a single async pull queue consumed by callers (for-await or ReadableStream sink). Under the hood it holds a reference to the current source (an AsyncIterable or a ReadableStream wrapper). Calls to swap(newSource, opts) atomically update the current source. If there are pending pullers, they are satisfied from the current source until it yields or is drained. Drain policy: 'drain' will allow the old source to finish emitting queued items before de-referencing it; 'drop' will immediately cancel the old source's AbortController and discard queued items.

Backpressure: we model backpressure by limiting an internal buffer (highWaterMark) and only pulling from the active source when buffer has capacity. For ReadableStream facade we implement pull() to rearm pulls into the adapter's queue. Cancellation: adapter owns an AbortController per source and a root AbortController. When the adapter is aborted the root signal aborts every active source and rejects pending pull promises.

Edge cases: swapping while a pending read is blocked, swapping to a source that is itself a ReadableStream (wrap using a small async iterator shim), swapping to sources that emit synchronously, and preserving order across composite transforms. We intentionally avoid reordering guarantees across sources: order is sourceA items followed (depending on policy) by sourceB items.

Instrumentation: expose light-weight metrics: swaps.count, swaps.duration, swap_drops.count, pending_pull_count, buffer_size_gauge. Integrate with SDK tracing so path of a request that triggered a swap is visible in console traces.
api_examples:
// Swap with drop policy to immediately favor new source
adapter.swap(newSource, { drainPolicy: 'drop' }); // cancels old source and starts new one
progress_updates: 2025-11-12: Ticket created. Captured recurring customer/internal ask: need to support mid-stream fallback without tearing down consumer.
2025-11-15: POC implemented (60 LOC) demonstrating swapping between two fetch-streams in browser. Verified for-await consumer still works.
2025-11-18: Design review with Ryan (infra) and Priya (PM). Agreed to add drainPolicy and root AbortController. Raised potential performance risk for high-frequency swaps.

2025-11-20: Added ReadableStream facade and Node wrapper for stream.Readable. Benchmarked simple swap scenario: median extra latency ~0.8ms per swap at 1k ops/sec with HWM=8. Recorded in experiment dashboard: https://dashboards.internal.redwood/streams/swap-exp-11
2025-11-24: PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/5123. Includes unit tests and two examples under examples/stream-swap.
2025-11-25: CI flaky on Node 14 with polyfill mismatch (streams/web polyfill). Investigating fallback polyfill and adjusting test harness. Leaving ticket In Progress until CI green.
testing_plan: Unit tests: swap semantics with drain vs drop, cancellation, pending-pull satisfaction, synchronous source yields
Integration tests: Node/Deno/Browser E2E using Playwright for browser scenarios and native fetch streams
Stress test: 10k swaps per second in a harness simulating bursty reconnects, verify memory usage and no leaks
Backpressure tests: consumer that pauses after N items to ensure adapter stops pulling from source until resumed
Compatibility: run existing stream bridge tests (ENG-56124 style) and add cross-runtime matrix in CI
Observability: assert metrics emitted for swaps and drops in test harness (local micrometrics)
Add sample apps: examples/stream-swap/fallback-app and examples/stream-swap/model-variant-switch
risks: Incorrect backpressure handling could cause head-of-line latency regressions for some customers
Memory leaks if old sources are not fully cancelled and hold references to closures
Pollyfills and runtime differences (Node 14 vs Node >=18 vs Deno vs browsers) may require multiple code paths and increase maintenance burden
Complexity for the public surface: keep API minimal to avoid user confusion (prefer swap(options) over many specialized calls)
